utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. On behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor, I'm Tom Hannis along with Jasmina Bosnjakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic, appearing for Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Our first witness today is Radovan Pejic. I would like to put one matter on the record before he comes in. I have had the registrar hand around a hard copy of a portion of Exhibit P1428. This is a log-book that came into evidence with the witness Dragan Kezunovic earlier. And that document was previously 65 ter 2516, and originally in e-court it only had 50 pages of the B/C/S of the log-book. Other portions of that same log-book were in e-court under other 65 ter numbers but we've now moved into P1428 the entire 400 and some pages of the B/C/S. So it's complete. I wanted you to know that. The hard copy I've given to you is because I intend to show the witness a few documents that I believe are listed in the hard copy portion of this document, and I think it will be easier for us to have a hard copy of the log-book while we put up on the screen copies of the exhibits that pertain thereto. I think it will be easier for all of us to work. That's why I've handed it around. I have also given it to the Defence along with a copy for their client. And with that, I'm ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, perhaps if I'm here long enough I will master this matter of entering exhibits and numbering them. Do I understand the position to be, that this is a working copy of -- of a -- of -- of a full Exhibit, that's my first question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct. This is the first 50 pages of an exhibit that is 420-some pages, I think, in the B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: My second question is whether the exhibit that has been entered has unnecessary pages to -- to simplify it, which should, for practical purposes, now be deleted to -- to tidy up the exhibit, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour I can take a look at that. I don't recall now the ending date in the B/C/S but certainly as far as I'm concerned anything after December 31st, 1992 or the first week in January probably can be deleted. But as I stand here for the moment I don't recall where 1993 ends. I know what you have before you takes us up to I think, early August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So at some point we can anticipate, can we, that the OTP who would have tendered this exhibit would perform the exercise, the tidying exercise and the Registry and the Chamber and everybody else would be put in the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And in relation to that I should indicate that at this point the only English translation that has been done is of the first ten or so pages. The 49 items that were listed under the portion of the log-book that was kept for MUP headquarters in Vrace between the 20-something of April and the 13th of May, I believe. But we will be obtaining an English translation of the portions of the log-book for CSB Sarajevo from June something 1992 when it begins through to the end of 1992. And then the rest we will remove or delete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So -- so you may call your - to borrow your words - first witness. I don't know if that was a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Your Honour. We call ST-160, Radovan Pejic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think I misspoke. For the record he's ST-168, and it looks like I said 160, I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I could be of assistance to my learned friend and the Trial Chamber. The P1428 the last entry of 1992 is under number 1813. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is there a date for that last entry?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 31 December 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But it has numbers from 1 until 1813 are the entries for 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Witness. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's very good. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your testimony. We will start by asking you to read the solemn declaration, which is being shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may sit down. And, sir, could we begin by asking you to state your full name and your date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Radovan Pejic. I was born on the 22nd of August, 1956, in a place called Jelasica, Kalinovik municipality, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And what's your profession today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm an inspector of the crime police in a team belonging to the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska for investigating war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And where are you posted at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The team has its headquarters in Pale, but in organisational terms it is directly linked to the cabinet of the minister and the police director.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, what was your occupation in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, I was an employee working in the militia or police, and I worked in the communications centre and the Security Services Centre until the tragic conflicts bloke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina when I transferred to what is today the MUP of the Republika Srpska in the communications centre of the MUP at Vrace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So you were transferred to Vrace in April 1992; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. And I worked as a communications operative as a signalsman in the centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you say in Vrace throughout 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stayed at Vrace. I was there in 1992, the beginning of 1992, and when the seat of the ministry moved from Vrace to Pale, or, rather, to Mount Jahorina, I then requested the chief of the Security Services Centre and the minister to allow me to remain in the Security Services Centre so I continued to work there in the department and for a relatively short period of time we stayed in Vrace and then moved for security reasons to Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, sir, is this your first testimony before this Tribunal? Have you ever given evidence before in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I'm testifying. I've never testified before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Have you testified in any domestic criminal proceedings about matters relating to the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Let me then explain to you briefly how the proceedings will unfold here. You have been called as a witness by the Prosecution, who is sitting to your right, and the Prosecution has asked for, all together, two-hours to examine you in-chief. After that, the counsel for Mr. Stanisic, sitting to your left, has asked for three hours to cross-examine you. And when Mr. Zecevic is through with his cross-examination, Mr. Pantelic, who is representing the other accused, Mr. Zupljanin has asked for one and a half hours to cross-examine you. And when Mr. Pantelic is through, we will give the floor back to the Prosecution who will have a chance to put some final questions to you, in light of the answers you have given through your cross-examination. And after that, and in between, the Judges, may, at all times, put questions to you. So that will be the end of your testimony. We hope that we can complete your testimony by tomorrow. Now, one practical matter. The recordings here are taken on videotape, and the tapes have to be changed every 90 minutes, so that means that every hour and a half we have to have a break. These breaks are about 20 minutes and then we continue. And the proceedings today will end at a quarter to 2.00 and then we will resume tomorrow at 9.00 in this courtroom. That's all I have to say except that I wish to remind you that now that you have taken the solemn declaration you are obliged to tell the truth, and I should remind you that there is a severe penalty for providing false or incomplete testimony to the Chamber here. Thank you very much. And I now give the floor to the Prosecution. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pejic. Judge Harhoff has covered most of it but I would like to ask you just a few further questions about your background leading up to the conflict and some of your work since then. Can you tell the Judges what your educational background was before you got to work for the police? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the secondary school for Internal Affairs at Vrace in the second generation in 1974. And immediately after that, I was sent to the Secretariat of the Interior in Novo Sarajevo, Sarajevo where I worked until 1978 when I transferred to the youth organisation in Novi Grad, a socio-political organisation, and there I occupied various posts right up until 1991 or rather, the multi-party selections in Bosnia and Herzegovina when I returned to the Security Services Centre in Sarajevo and the department for encryption and communications. During my regular schooling, in addition to gaining the necessary training for a trainee policeman, I went to a specialist course for photography or, rather, crime technology and within the framework of my working activities I also attended an encryption course which allowed me to take the professional examination and be sent to the security services centre and communications centre of Sarajevo. I have engaged in politics from the youth association and from my youth association membership there, and then on I was executive secretary member of the Presidency of various organisations and after the conflict broke out in addition to communications I also dealt with analytics and informatics, and for a time I worked as a journalist analyst. In the meantime I graduated from the London school for media relations and was deployed to the post of the head of the bureau for relations with the public of the MUP of Republika Srpska. Upon completion or after the elections for the new government and the new minister I was sent back to the team to investigate war crimes and that is something that we reached an agreed about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I understand from your answers to Judge Harhoff that immediately before the conflict broke out in April 1992, you were working in the communications centre of the -- the joint or the pre-war MUP in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when did you go to Vrace to work for the newly formed Serbian MUP and later it was called the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: I arrived at Vrace on the 6th of April. However, I would like to explain something. One month prior to that, or maybe a little more, the chief of the department for communications and encryption of the Security Services Centre, of Sarajevo Mr. Zlatan Sehovic was his name and his deputy Draskovic, Slavko, Slavko Draskovic held a meeting with all the communications officers, and we were briefly told that there was certain political events afoot and unrest and that most probably the ministry would -- of the interior would be divided. That is to say, the minister of the republic of BH divided into at least two parts, and we were told that we shouldn't pay any attention to those events but that we should act in a highly responsible and professional manner and conscientiously carry out our tasks linked to communications and that the leaders would see to other matters and take care that on the schedules and occupying all posts in the communications department there would not be just a mono ethnic composition but that we would all be represented, Serbs, Croats, Muslims or rather, Bosniaks so that quite simply it didn't matter if the ministry was split, if the MUP was split. It didn't matter which minister was signing the documents, that all information had to be sent out in a highly professional manner to the addressees, and at one point I think it was between the 3rd and 4th of April, during the night, on the night shift I remained alone on all the positions in the communications and encryption department which was set up in various offices, on the ground floor and on the first floor, and when I didn't know what to do, I contacted the chief of the department, who was Zlatan, and he called me to come to the teleprinter and encryption centre where he was, where he came to, and then he explained to me that his colleagues allegedly received information according to which that very night the municipal SUP, which was where our seat was, would be targeted and that our colleagues for that reason had left their job, left their work posts, and then in front of me, he would call out the names of each one of them and said, Now, if you received that kind of information, why didn't you inform [indiscernible] but why did you leave him all alone? So he told me that the safest thing for me to do was in the morning to spend as much time in the encryption cubicle which was a safe place, secure place specially built to cater to fire and untoward events, and so in the morning when I finished my duty and shift, I was allowed to go home and then at the entrance I saw that there were -- that none of my colleagues were there anymore, no security details. And that the people who were there then were people I didn't know, and that made me decide not go back to work. I contacted Draskovic. He told me to report to the new centre at Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could -- I appreciate that you wanted to explain all that to us, but can you try and -- and keep your answers short, limit them to my question. If you do need to add more, I certainly am willing to let you do that if you advise me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And also, could you show down because what you say has to be interpreted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. I only have two hours for my time so that's why I have to try and limit you. Also I think the interpreters are requesting that you slow down because you're speaking pretty rapidly for them. Okay?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So, Slavko Draskovic is the one who told you to report to Vrace. When you went there on April 6th, who did you speak to? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of April, in the communications centre, I met my colleague, Mr. Trifkovic, and then on the following day, I had conversation with the chief of administration or assistant minister for communications, Mr. Kezunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Obrad Trifkovic is the colleague you meant?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: That's right. Communications officers who had worked in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Kezunovic was Dragan Kezunovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: That's right, Dragan Kezunovic. He was assistant of the minister for communications and encryption.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you arrived at Vrace on the 6th of April, 1992, what -- what communications equipment did you -- did you find available to use at that location?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: At the time, there was only one functional phone that was connected to the switchboard but the switchboard wasn't functioning because of the large number of local links that were short-circuited. There was some damage to the system we have had, also one fixed radio station, and some mobile radio stations that were part of the equipment of the special and traffic brigade from Vrace. And the remainder of material we got only later, and we also had some field telephones that were connected to the guard posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have any teletype machines?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: There was a teletype machine, but it wasn't operational because the node for its function was located in the CSB in Sarajevo, and they had been made unoperational, at least for the area that belonged to MUP of RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We've heard the terms KT, which I think translates into English as short wave and UKT ultra short wave. Can you explain, first of all, for me, the difference between KT and UKT?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: High frequency stations HF work on high frequencies have big range. There is no need to use repeaters, they have their own antennas for transmission. This antenna is just taken to an appropriate place, then one makes a calculation in order to see how far it needs to reach and it can actually send messages, as we say, to the other part of the world. The HF or very high frequency radio stations are divided into fixed and mobile. They use very high frequencies, ultra high frequencies, and what they need is to have connection with places which are visibly visible to them. If they hit some kind of obstacle the wave changes directions and they cannot be used for communication. To make them operational, one needs repeaters. In this case they were at Trebevic, but that was not something that could be done through the CSB because it could be done only after a code was typed in the base. Why? Because in the UHF frequency we have communication using two lines, one for transmission, the other one for reception, except when one is using the Simplex principle, when you have to have optical visibility. In semi-Duplex, you need to have optical visibility only to the repeater.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if I understand correctly, you said the repeater was located on Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was that -- and in April 1992, was that an area under control of the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Physically, yes, Trebevic was under our control.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you able to use that -- that relay station or repeater for your communications from Vrace in April, May, June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: For the first few days, yes. But after that date, my colleagues from the centres, very often, would, when we would be using this link, switch off the repeaters and in attempts to find a good solution we went to Trebevic myself and a colleague of mine, and we switched off the repeaters and instead of the repeaters we introduced the most reliable mode of communication, a man, who used two station to -- with one station repeat -- receive the communication and then the other one to send the message. In order to prevent any kind of incursions into our system we set up a code table, and we could also recognise the person by the voice and then we could say, This voice is something that may be transferred. Our colleagues from the CSB immediately noticed what we had done and they used the so-called war reserves. I knew about the existence of the equipment. They put the antennas of their repeaters on the high buildings and started using them. We worked in such a way that somebody had to -- a person had to be there next to the repeater to maintain it. However, this communication functioned only for the region of Sarajevo, rather, for the area where there is optical visibility between the repeater's antenna and the user. For instance, towards Zvornik, Han Derventa, there was an evaluation. Beneath that was Ilidza, Hadzici, Ilijas. This was what we could cover but nothing further than the region of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about contact with Pale? What kind of communication links did you have between Vrace and Pale in April, May, June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: In addition to the UHF link and I don't remember when this was, I think maybe in late April or early May, at the time of our transfer to Lukavica we also got VHF communication. These two modes of communications with Pale were reliable but we also used phone lines when there was electricity in Lukavica or in Pale which was more often the case in Pale, and the phones were an efficient means of communications only after the phone switchboard at the school of economics was made functional. In addition to that, before the airport was transferred to the international forces or the United Nations, we managed to put three telephone lines from Ilidza and connect them because they were something that we also used in the CSB. We started obtaining fax machines or started using the ones that were there at Vrace. We also received some from various companies or if someone had tried to steal such a machine then police at their check-points would seize it from them and that equipment would also be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall how many fax machines you had at Vrace in April, May, and June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: No. But if one's talking about dispatch communications, that was registered, but there wasn't much of that kind of correspondence because the fax machine in the Department of Interior Affairs is something that not an official mode of communications between organs of the interior because, according to regulations, information should be sent through dispatch communication means, meaning the teletype machine, which was put into function only later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how much later that happened?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: The first VHF devices equipment in our centre, we received them in late April/early May. But they were used mostly for the training and for the checkups, to see how things will work. Some of the stations that did not move their seat, such as Ilidza, Ilijas, and Vogosca, also had VHF equipment, and after several days of checkups, we could start using open communications. However, not the encrypted or closed protected communications. We waited for additional equipment, the so-called TG devices that could be linked up with VHF equipment and teletype machines and in such way one would be able to send written communications both in open and closed form, and only later other police stations in the area got the equipment but the communication with MUP was functioning, providing, of course, there was electrical power because not all the centres had generators. We got that only in June or July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition to this various kinds of equipment and means of communication, did you also, when necessary, make use of human beings as couriers when you weren't otherwise able to transmit a message by phone or fax or teleprinter, or radio?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Of course. An order was issued that if anyone's coming to the area of the CSB must report to the communications centre, and then we would give them envelopes with all the dispatches we've failed to send until that time, because the courier is the most reliable means of communications. But that mode of communication also implied delays because physically speaking from Lukavica to Ilidza it is necessary only to pass by the airport. However, because that route was closed, it was necessary to go first to Rajlovac then Vogosca all the way around Pale and Trebevic before reaching Lukavica, which is about 160 or 170 kilometres off a route, and the other way it would have been only about 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, thank you. I'd like to show you now an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is P573.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this is a document dated the 29th of June, 1992. It's a performance report for the period April to June 1992 for the Ministry of the Interior. And you see the cover page there. I would like to go to page 13 in the B/C/S in e-court. And that's page 8 of the English. Mr. Pejic the part I'd like you to look at is the full paragraph in the middle of the page, immediately above the number 2. I'll read from my English translation and ask you a question. It says: "At this point" - 29 June, I guess - "the minister of the interior had its headquarters in Pale uses public telephone and telefax communication systems to maintain contact with the Security Services Centres in Banja Luka Bijeljina and Sarajevo. And short wave systems for contact with Trebinje and Sarajevo CSBs." I'll skip a sentence. It says: "An ultra short-wave link has been established with the Sarajevo CSB because technical conditions existed for that." Does that conform with your memory of the situation at the end of June 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that this is a true account of the conditions in the communications centre of the CSB centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did the RS move offices or headquarters from Vrace to Pale? Do you remember approximately when that took place?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: I think it was in late May or early June when the preparations started, and, after that, was when MUP moved and the CSB moved to Lukavica about ten days after that. I cannot give you exact dates. This is to the best of my memory. But I think it was -- I know it was in late May or early June, because we didn't have proper working conditions at Vrace although we were in the facilities of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at Lukavica, I take it that's where you went when the move took place. You didn't go to Pale, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: I did not. As I've already explained, thanks to the understanding of the minister and the chief of the CSB, my request was approved and the chief proposed to the minister that I be appointed the chief of encryption and communication in CSB, and immediately after my appointment I started preparing the facilities. Lukavica is only several kilometres away from Vrace. We were not immediately at the demarcation lines or combat lines, unlike Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your CSB chief was Mr. Cvetic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Late Zoran Cvetic, whom I met upon my arrival in Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at Lukavica, what -- what equipment did you find available to be used when you moved there? Just briefly and generally.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: We moved high frequency and ultra high frequency equipment we had at Vrace, and we also set up phones, because, by then, the school of economics switchboard was already functional. We made sure that we had sufficient number of phone lines for fax and mediation needs. Also, for a time, we used several phones that belonged to the other side but they would very soon detect us doing it and they would switch them off. We, for a while, had three federal numbers, but as soon as they would realize there was a lot of communication using those lines, because they were listening in, they would realize that it's us using it and they would switch it off either by switching it off or cutting the lines. We had a reliable phone line, or, rather, two numbers which went from Ilidza to Lukavica, from the post office switchboard at Ilidza, since this area was throughout the period under the RS MUP control.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. We've seen a payroll document from May 1992 where there's a Radovan Pejic listed as working in the analytical section. Is that you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And to avoid any misunderstanding, this is the very period when I, as a communications officer, based on the order by the minister and his assistant, was charged with some analytical tasks, and that's when I had medial co-operation with Mr. Petar Vujicic. Once we would get the bulletins in the morning as a communications officer, I could have done it on my own but formally speaking analysts were to do that work, and then I compiled a bulletin that was then through the ministry sent to the highest leaders in Republika Srpska but because the distribution in the CSB was already underway, it was clear that the request would be granted. There was a, in principle, agreement between the officials and that's why I could be found on both lists because the list was not done at the end of the month but in the -- very first day of the following month.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How long did you remain in your position as -- as chief of communications for the Sarajevo CSB?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Until our move to Ilidza. And I think that was in 1994. In 1994, I was sent to Ilidza to start the preparations for the transfer of CSB into the premises of the SJB at Ilidza. Upon arrival in Ilidza, I worked in the encryption and communication unit of the station and prepared for the arrival of other services.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand at the beginning of the conflict in early April when the separation occurred that you had a shortage of qualified communications people on the Serbian side; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Some of our colleagues failed to leave in time, and later, when they wanted, they could not. Vrbarac Srdjan confirmed that who joined us in the department in only 1995. They didn't simply expect things to develop so -- and were unable to reach the MUP of Republika Srpska. They stayed working down there for a long time, but once the conditions were ripe, they also left. But there were very few of us that were in our area that was under our control and the same applies to the people who were in charge of maintenance of the communications. But, initially, in the seat at least, the situation was slightly better than with the maintenance people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: To make up for this shortage, did you hire new employees to fill the gap?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... personally as a chief of coms in CSB Sarajevo, or did it require higher approval?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: The procedure is very specifically prescribed. In case of communications officer, there are some -- more specific requirements. I could identify the person who was capable of being a communications officer, the person would first be interviewed. Then I would make a proposal with an explanation and pass it on to the chief of centre, who would then pass it on to the minister, asking for a person to be appointed to such and such a position and such and such a department. And once the conditions were there, we abided by this procedure and, no, I could not hire anyone but I could influence in my proposal who is -- who should be appointed. So also before the minister has approved it, the assistant for communications and encryption also has to approve the person. The minister wouldn't sign anything without the approval, prior approval of the assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this -- this system that required approval of the minister, was that true only for communications employees or for all MUP employees; if you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: According to the law, people can be hired and appointed into the service only by the minister. There is prescribed procedure and conditions under which people can be hired by MUP. At certain point, members of the reserve police force were, based on their work time assignments, included into the MUP stations, and these issues were only later resolved by either appointing these people into the ministry or dismissing them. The practice is even now like that, namely the director of the police is also entitled to sign some of the appointment decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. When you went to Vrace on the 6th of April, during that first month in April, who -- who else was there in the Serbian MUP? Who were the senior staff, if any, present at Vrace?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Very often when he was not somewhere in the field or elsewhere, the minister of the interior was at Vrace and his assistants as well and deputies, unless, of course, they were somewhere out in the field, because the official seat of the ministry at the time was at Vrace and all the accompanying services were being set up at that location. There was also the special police unit located there under the command of Mr. Karisik. In addition to the ministry seat, there was the centre's seat and the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Centre, CSB Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: At the time it was called Sarajevo-Romanija-Birac centre because we covered considerably larger area than the one of the Sarajevo region. We had Zvornik, Sarajevo -- Bratunac, Visegrad, and Foca under our area. The organisation didn't match the earlier peacetime organisation. It was extended to a larger period, and it covers larger period than it covers today, because at the time we had to take over some of the stations that are now linked up with Bijeljina. Then we took over all the stations of the CSB Gorazde that were in the hands of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall was Momcilo Mandic in Vrace in April 1992 when you were there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Momcilo Mandic, as far as I remember, wasn't an employee of the MUP then. He worked for the Ministry of Justice. The seat of that ministry was not at Vrace, but, rather at Kula or Pale where the government was, but he did come to Vrace occasionally. I would see him there, but he didn't have his workplace there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We've seen some evidence suggesting that Mr. Mandic became minister of justice in mid or late May 1992. You're not aware of him holding a position in the RS MUP before that, in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: I don't know what position he had in the MUP at that time. I know that in the RS UP he was one of the top executives of the crime police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. While at Vrace, I think you told us that you worked as a communications officer, and I understand that part of your duties involved sending and receiving dispatches. Did you also work on the telephone, answering the phone?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: As there were only two of us working, depending on how much we could stand, we would work all the time and take shifts. Of course, I did everything needed. I sent out and received dispatches and I was in charge of UHF and phone communications because the switchboard was not functional at the very beginning. So this was a huge burden because if anyone wanted to speak to the minister he had to go and fetch him personally. Only later were we able to get the switchboard working so that we could put calls through.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. In connection with that, I would like to show you a couple of exhibits already in evidence and ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The first is P1146, which is at tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think this is a document that you've seen before. It's a transcript of an intercepted telephone conversation on the 23rd of April, 1992. Speakers listed are Radovan Pejic and Radovan Karadzic. You recognise that as a transcript you looked at before?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it before. And I heard the audio recording. So I can certify that this conversation is authentic. I, indeed, spoke to the president then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you were in Vrace at the time of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know where Mr. Karadzic was calling from?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: At that time, we were not able to identify incoming calls. Only later was the switchboard equipped to do that. But I can suppose that it was an incoming call from Pale to Vrace. I believe that Pale was the -- was the place from which the call originated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. As I understand it, you said that it was necessary, in the early days, to leave the switchboard and go upstairs in the building to get the minister or others to come down, because there was not an internal phone connection. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: That is right. Only later were we able to equip the switchboard to do that. And that is probably why the president was talking to me here rather than to the minister because everybody knew what the conditions of work at Vrace were like.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show you 65 ter number 2399 now. This is at tab 2. Mr. Pejic, this relates to the issue of telephone links and telephone communications. This is a document that you've seen before, and it purports to be a pre-war schematic diagram of the telephone links within the pre-war MUP. Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the schematic shows our functioning before the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, when the war broke out, the link in Sarajevo were broken because much of the confrontation line was running throughout and around Sarajevo, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the main hub was also at the RSUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what the situation was in Banja Luka centre with regard to its telephone links with subordinate SJBs as shown on this chart? Do you know whether that remained intact in 1992, after the war started?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: I have no precise information, but I suppose that provided they had power in there, then they could have internal communications, but as for other communications, no. That is, from the centre toward the stations, in my assumption, unless there were other technical problems from the purely technical side communication was possible. Of course, all the other preconditions had to be met that the -- all the devices had to have, power supply, uninterrupted power supply, and -- but most of the stations remained linked in Banja Luka. However, I'm not familiar with the exact state of affairs in that centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours I'd like to tender 2399.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1471, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Pejic, I have a question for you. There's been some evidence that pre-war during a one-year period there may have been hundreds of thousands of dispatches sent out by the MUP headquarters. And in the annual report for the RS MUP, which we'll look at later, the number is a very much low number. Just in general terms, can you tell me, during the war time conditions in the RS MUP, there were certain categories of dispatches which had been commonly sent in the pre-war period that were no longer being sent as dispatches during 1992 in the war period? Do you follow my question?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I think that the information that you put forward can be interpreted as a conservative assessment. Because before the war, dispatches that went from the RSUP towards the centres and the police stations could include 100 or 200 dispatches in one packet, because dispatches are used to inform the relevant institutions of all security relevant events, such as stolen vehicles and what have you, whereas -- dispatches relating to lower-level operative matters were not so numerous in war time. 8 But it was to be expected that the number of dispatches about security- 9 relevant events would be much greater, and in my view, had the communication 10 lines functioned well, it would be at least equal to the quantities in 11 peacetime, if not greater. Such information was however mostly transmitted 12 by phone or in direct contact between the officers, and dispatches were used 13 only when necessary although that wasn't strictly in accordance with the 14 rules, but events happened so fast that almost on an hourly basis there would 15 have had to be dispatches arriving to the Center, and then from the Center to 16 the MUP, dispatches about combat activities or other security-relevant 17 events. But I believe that the officers in charge compensated for that 18 through telephone communication or through other types of contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. We asked you to generally describe for us the procedure in 20 the communications centre that MUP headquarters in Vrace and in your CSB 21 Sarajevo later on, can you briefly describe the procedure for how dispatches 22 is drafted and sent out? Can you go through the steps that take place? Say the minister wants to send some kind of decision or order to the CSBs and all the SJBs, how would that take place?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: When a dispatch is drafted, and it must include all the elements such as the prescribed form, the heading, the indication of urgency and the indication of confidentiality, who was supposed to receive it. Then somebody receives the dispatch, be it the courier or the secretary inspects the dispatch but not the content, they check the upper right corner where the chief and the dispatch distribution centre has to sign, and the urgency indication. And then they are ordered in the sequence of urgency. The last ones to be dealt with were the ones marked O, for open. And the MUP is duty-bound to -- to -- transmit them to the recipients but through the CSBs. If the dispatch was to be sent to all police stations, that is SJBs, then the communications officer at the CSB will register that dispatch as received and forward it to the stations. That is, the communications centre of the MUP cannot communicate directly in that case with an SJB but has to go through the communications centre of the CSB. The same applies to the communications from the police stations to the MUP of the RS. Exceptionally when there is a dispatch attended only for one SJB we can relay it directly as an intermediary. But, as a rule no dispatch would go to an SJB without the CSB being informed. That is why everything went through the CSB because one copy is kept there for information of the management of the centre. Because the MUP of the RS, even then - and now, too - was a centralised organisation, a hierarchical organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Concerning the levels of urgency I think we heard before that a designation very urgent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: As usual, when witnesses tell us how the system should work, it's always useful to ask if it actually did work. And my question to you, Mr. Pejic, is, if you can tell us just briefly, if the system which you have now described to us, how did it work in practice in the period between April and July 1992? Are you able to shed some light over this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Depending on the circumstances, we often had to wait for days for a dispatch to be transmitted to far away police stations or newly established police stations, such as Milici, until we put in place VHF devices. Those dispatches would most times wait for couriers. But we did whatever we could to transmit them as soon as possible, but remote police stations did have to wait for weeks, and then the information would mostly be obsolete. But we tried to be resourceful and have a vehicle going in that direction, carry it, or if the phone lines could be used and we used them, but the facts about the dispatch communications confirm what I said. In April and May, the situation was worse, was the worst but when we introduced teleprinters then it got better. Then -- we -- the communication lines were more stable from that time on. Of course, all provided that there was uninterrupted power supply. All systems would go down when the power plant was -- broke down and the generator only could work for 24 hours because these switchboards were from before the war, so you can imagine what this situation was like with the switchboards in Pale and Ilidza which were even older. If I compare that with the conditions -- with the pre-war conditions, our compatibility of efficiently transmitting information wasn't even 10 per cent of our capability before the war. If I had a dispatch to be sent out to all police station, I had to get -- establish contact with that police station physically whereas before the war it was enough to depress 20 or 30 buttons and no matter -- whether they were communicating with each other I would interrupt that communication and send out everything to all of them at the same time. Now the workload was 20 times greater. When the dispatches were of the open type we sometimes had to dictate the text to the recipient and especially if the dispatch was drafted by somebody who was not versed in that and it wasn't brief, but was put in the -- everything was explained at great length, and sometimes we will to use the most -- the simplest code which is S1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, I would ask my learned friend to instruct the witness to talk slowly because I have -- I have identified at least ten mistakes in the transcript what he says. That happened on page 24, 25, now it happened in his last answer. Because he -- in his answers he is giving so many details and it's impossible, I understand it is impossible for the interpreters to cover each and every -- each and every thing that the witness said. I will clarify this during the cross-examination, I just wanted the record to show that there is -- because we can ask for the verification request, but I don't want to complicate because I know what the witness said, and I will clarify that in my cross. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. And, Mr. Pejic, this will be yet another forceful reminder to you to speak slowly. I have also noticed that you actually speak very fast, but it's no good if the interpreters cannot follow you. So, please, bear in mind that you have to speak slowly and distinctly. Thank you. Back to you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic if you allow me, we all have to bear in mind that it is an interpretation and not translation that we are dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, but the point of the matter is I'm not -- I'm not saying that -- that each and every word needs to be interpreted but -- but instead of what -- what witness said one thing instead of that something else was recorded in the transcript. That -- and there are distinct things and it really makes the transcript very unclear, and it's not what the witness said. That is what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Pejic, perhaps it is partly because of your background as a communications worker, but I'm also told sometimes I talk too fast. We'll both try to slow down, and we only have three minutes before the first break. Let me ask you, with regard -- you mentioned not having teletype or teleprinter capability in many locations in the beginning of the conflict. If, in April or May you needed to send a coded dispatch somewhere and you did not have the teletype/teleprinter connection or capability, what means would you use to send a coded dispatch? Could you do it by radio or Morse code or on the telephone speaking, using some kind of common code? What would you do?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: The dispatches rated as -- as strictly confidential in April were coded by the so-called S1 encryption system. That is the oldest encryption system where every character of a word is represented by five characters in the code. So it is not important when you're doing that, whether you will transmit to -- that dispatch to the other side on the phone or not because whoever listens in does not have the code table and doesn't know what any character stands for. Another way we used was the so-called code book, which -- in which words are --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat this technical explanation. We can't follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I need to stop you because the interpreters have just intervened and asked if you can repeat but I see it is almost the time for the break, maybe we should break and I'll ask the question again when we resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Pejic, your last answer, in part, mentioned the so-called S1 encryption system which I understand to be a system where each letter of the plain text is represented by a code assisting of five symbols for that one letter, five for one substitution system. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then you started to mention that you also used the so-called code book. Could you slowly tell us what that was?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: It's a table, code book or code table, which sets out the main words, and surrounding that you have numbers and letters. And by crossing numbers which, when we send out this to each other, if anybody unauthorized were to come in they could make no sense of it. And then we provide a key so that when one of our colleagues receives a message of that kind he knows where to start. He has the key. He knows how to read it, how to read from left onwards or the top of the table or whatever. And when on the left-hand column at the top he sees an A, if there's a number 5 crossed with those two lines, he would get a word. When he puts all the words together, all that's needed is to correct the text in the sense of any grammatical or case variations. And there was the old principle of encoding too. People who knew this knew that coding system was rather old, out of date. Because it was too slow, in actual fact. Not because it was not reliable but because it was too slow and encryption has gone far ahead and it's easier to work with. But, any way, closed communication, the system of closed communication in the Ministry of the Interior implies that when information is forwarded or conveyed, it should not be detected and uncovered by others. For example, the very next day, the minister can repeat that in his report publicly, or make a public announcement, but when it is sent out, nobody must know the contents of such a message.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned earlier the -- the urgency ratings. And I've understood that very urgent is the highest level of urgency for sending messages; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Very urgent, according to the rules governing the system of encryption in the MUP, which we inherited from the RSUP or, rather, the federal SUP of the former Yugoslavia, implied that from the moment of reception of such a dispatch in the communications centre in the space of 30 minutes that dispatch would have to have been sent out to the addressee, as a rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And apart from the situation where you have urgent circumstances like your police station being attacked, who, in the MUP, had the authority to send messages -- or draft messages as being very urgent? Could anybody in the MUP do that, or was it limited to certain positions?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: The rules govern that, when you have a very urgent dispatch, it is only the minister or the individual he authorises, with the exception of cases -- well, since the rules were taken over from peacetime conditions, when there's an aggression, for example, against Yugoslavia, then in that case, the leader of the organisational unit which noticed this phenomenon happening or a piece of interesting security information going to the minister could use the very urgent code. Usually it refers -- it is placed -- very urgent is placed to secure -- to matters of great interest to security and so on and so forth going to the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could your CSB chief designate a message as being very urgent?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, in exceptional circumstances. If, for example, there was an attack on Vrace or something like that. But as far as I remember, the chief of the centre, the CSB chief, did not use that marking but used the code tables and he could also orally via those code tables, convey the information in the proper way. But officials lower down the pecking order in Republika Srpska such as the assistant minister, the chiefs of the Security Services Centre and so on and so forth, they would use something else and that was DD. It was also a very precise mark which meant from one hour to a maximum of three hours that was the leeway given for forwarding, and it was used most frequently because all the chiefs were well-acquainted with the possibilities and capacities of the communications centre and that is why they avoided using too many -- sending out too many dispatches of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Related to that, I have a question about the process. The situation where maybe you get a dispatch that's coded DD and either you don't have enough time to get it sent within the required limit or the line is not functioning, you have no power or the line's been cut or the operator on the other end is not answering the radio, what was the process within the communications centre in such a circumstance where you were unable to deliver a message as requested? What were you supposed to do under the rules?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Under the rules within a certain deadline we would resort to all means possible to have the dispatch forwarded to the addressee stipulated. And then we would record that in our log-book of received and sent-out dispatches. Similarly, either on the back page or the front page, if there's enough space, we would record that on the original dispatch as well that arrived at the communications centre, and we would write down the time, the hour and the minute, when the dispatch was handed over. Let me give you an example. To the police station of Ilijas. Now, if we failed to send it to the Ilidza police station, then we would write down a note, a remark, saying that it had been copied, put into an envelope and was waiting for a courier, and then a copy of the dispatch in that way would be returned to the author once the deadline expires and then the author -- it is up to the author to decide what he is going to do, whether he is going do send it out late, by courier, or if the time-limit has expired and it is no longer topical, then, he will tell the person who returns the dispatch to him to withdraw all the copies that were prepared for the courier, or to write on those copies that it is just by way of information, a piece of information so that the person opening the envelope knows that it's out of date but, nevertheless, it provides a certain amount of information which might be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess, to ask the question that Judge Harhoff would ask. You've described this as how it was supposed to work under the rules. Is that how it actually worked in real life when you worked at Vrace and when you were in the CSB communications centre for Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely the way I've described it, but most of those dispatches were left to be dispatched by courier. We succeeded in transmitting most of them by other forms of communication -- we were not successful in transmitting them by other means of communication much, but mostly by courier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In terms of reporting within the RS MUP, did the SJBs have an obligation to report up to headquarters through the -- through the centres information about police activities, in particular, police involvement in combat activities in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Upon arrival at Vrace, we would, at least in the communications centre, and later on, as I worked as an analyst as well, we would apply documents from peacetime which related to the specific area we were dealing. However, because of the new cadres coming into the police stations, we realized that many of the people coming in did not have any knowledge of this, didn't know how to do it, so as far as I remember, as soon as necessary conditions were created a large instructive dispatch was sent out, a dispatch with instructions stating what needed to be done on a daily basis, what needed to be done on a weekly basis, monthly basis and so on, half-year, one-year, et cetera, how to report back to the centre, and once the centre had collected all these reports it would send out a report to the MUP headquarters. Later on this dispatch with instructions was translated, if I remember correctly. Well, it became instructions called instructions on obligatory daily, weekly, reporting and reporting within various time spans according to the different areas about the situation -- the employee situation, about combat, about regular police affairs and the like, other important information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what the requirement was regarding reports about combat activity? Was that required to be reported daily, weekly, monthly?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Combat reports or reports on combat activity were sent out at all those times, daily, weekly and sometimes monthly, et cetera, and that implied that the centre would be informed of how many police members were at what positions of defence and how many had taken part in combat, how much time they had spent up at those positions, whether there were any wounded or killed, whether there were any movements in the lines, if the lines were attacked, and whether or not control -- they managed to regain control of the lines if there was shifting. Now, as a rule, as far as I know, our members in the special units, special police units, took part -- they came from all organisational units and went as re-enforcements to the Army of Republika Srpska where needed on a regular basis. And very often they also had to be deployed in providing assistance where the defence lines were under threat, and the policemen then were withdrawn from their regular duties and sent out as reenforcements to the army units, where needed. And in the bulletin, which was sent out in the morning, the centre would have to be informed about all this and then we would collect up all the information for our given area and then send it on to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not request from the -- the SJBs or subordinate units request to engage police members in combat activity had to be sent to the CSBs in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: No. I think that, especially when the system of communications functioned poorly, the decisions had to be made by officers in those police stations, by the chiefs of the police stations, and the requests, if I understood some reports from the stations correctly, they would get them either from the army directly or through the Crisis Staffs which had been established in the municipalities. And let me emphasise once again, if I understood the information we received correctly because I read the reports as somebody working as an analyst, in part. I say this because a communications officer never looks at the contents of information. He doesn't deal with the contents. He ex officio is not interested in context. All his job requires is for him to forward the information, so I'm saying this from the aspects of my job as an analyst, and it follows that the Crisis Staffs in their respective areas without the knowledge of the ministry could engage them but, of course, the junior commander was duty-bound as soon as conditions were ripe to inform the centre and then the centre would inform the ministry, up the chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, then, in your position in 1992, you did see reports from subordinate police organisational units such as SJBs coming into the CSB, and these reports were about requests from either the army or the Crisis Staff for the engagement of police units in combat, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes. It said in the reports. For example, that at the request of the Crisis Staff of Ilidza, for instance, because of an attack on Nedzarici at such and such a period of time, so many policemen were sent as reenforcement to the reserve police force in Nedzarici and that they took part in the defence of that particular territory. Now whether they managed to do that the same day while the attack was ongoing, and that was rarely possible, then it was done as soon as the attacks stopped, or rather, as soon as conditions permitted and that you had the time to write out information and reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understand that the CSBs had a requirement to send daily reports to MUP headquarters. Yes?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That was done in keeping with the dispatch with instructions coming from the ministry through the so-called bulletin of daily events.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did those daily reports from the CSBs include information about the combat activities in the subordinate SJBs? That's the type of information you would include and forward to the ministry.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did include that. And at the end of the bulletin, it always stated from what public security stations information did not come in for that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I want to go -- I'm going to jump around a little bit. I want to show you a few documents and ask you some specific questions about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The first one is 65 ter number 360. It's at tab 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Pejic, this is a document dated 20 May 1992. It's addressed to all security service centres, to the chief. It has the stamped title and -- and name of minister of the interior Mico Stanisic and somebody's signature. My question relates to the last sentence. It's a request for certain kinds of information to be broken down by public security station about the number of police, the number of stations, et cetera. And the last line says: "Information to be submitted by courier by 5 June at the latest." Is this unusual to have a request from the minister to send information by courier instead of by dispatch or some other means?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: In this particular case if we look at what is being requested then it is not unusual because although this document does not have a confidentiality rating, the answers to the questions posed would present the top security rating and would have to be top secret or strictly confidential. Because, quite simply, somebody -- some unauthorised person -- if it fell into the hands of some unauthorised person - these answers, I mean - then the person would gain complete insight into cadres, organisation, and so on of the MUP of the Republika Srpska, all its potential. And it would not be possible for one centre to summarise all this information for all the centres and units and compile a report which could be sent out in dispatch form. And that is why, I think, that this was resorted to in this case that it was decided to send a courier, send it by courier, and quite possibly, this document did not go through the communications centre, or even if it did, it might have been sent by regular post; but it could also go as an open dispatch because it was common knowledge that a leader, a -- who wanted to establish or build up an institution would necessarily have to know all the data set out here. So -- and nothing that is being requested here in this form is a secret, because the other side was organised in similar fashion, identically, and they were well aware of the fact that this was how the MUP of RS was organised although they might not know the number of police stations, for example, or the number of regulars or reservists without going into further details contained in this document. Therefore, using this specific example it is not unusual to submit the information by courier. But, as I said, the establishment system provides for this possibility because the couriers would take regular post which did not go through the communications centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1472, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, Mr. Pejic, I'd like to show you a log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is 65 ter number 2577, and it's at tab 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you saw a hard copy of this before. And my question was, if you were able to identify where this log-book would be from, based on -- on the contents in terms of what the messages are and to whom they're delivered. Do you recall looking at this one?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: I do recall, and I think that during the proofing for today I managed to identify with a degree of reliability that this is the log-book of the Ilijas SJB; I think their mark was 17-7. But, based on some names mentioned in the log-book, I think I can say that this is about the area of Ilijas because the surname, Popic and Subotic, hail from there. And I think the employment lists are being sent for this organisational unit because who else would be doing that? So, yes, I think it's the Ilijas Public Security Station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to tender 2577, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What Mr. Hannis is the effect of this document in your submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ilijas is one of our listed municipalities, communication continues to be a contested issue in this case. There are certain entries where there are references to document numbers that we think we're able to link up with other documents which are in or will be in evidence later on, and we think it's part of our burden of proof to show that there was communication with the Ilijas SJB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I think that was obvious with the last two exhibits. This ... this was a supplemental -- what you are saying is this is supplemental to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- this is a particular police station, we haven't got a lot of witnesses about Ilijas, and what this [indiscernible] necessary to show the communications link with this municipality we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1473, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, Mr. Pejic, I'd like to show you 65 ter 2914.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is at tab 23, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is another one you will have looked at before. It is dated 18 June 1992 from the Ministry of Defence, addressed to ministries of the government indicating that the communications centre at Pale can send telegrams to the Serb Autonomous Region of Bosanski Krajina and to other Serbian Autonomous Regions. Did you see this document in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: I didn't receive this document in official form, either from Ministry of Defence or the Ministry of the Interior. It is possible that I have seen it in my contacts with my colleagues in the military communications centre of the RS in Lukavica because by that date, I already worked in the communications centre of the CSB, and I can say that that particular communications centre was not using this form of communication. Now, whether some other organs of the ministry may have used it through Kalovita Brda location at Pale, of that I don't know anything. So I do not know whether MUP of Republika Srpska used this possibility of communication at all. Communication with Bosanski Krajina, if we needed to establish communication with them, we, as the centre, could achieve by sending them first to the MUP communication centre, now whether they would simply forward it or use the military communications systems, I don't know. In the period when I was working in the period of April and May, when I was working in the MUP communications centre, we didn't have this option. We did not send a single dispatch in that period or forward any dispatch at the time, any dispatch towards Krajina. And here I'm referring to the Vrace communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, were -- even though you didn't do that were you aware of the possibility, the offer of the use of those communication facilities to the MUP where that was a possible alternative means that was available?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: As a chief of department in the Security Services Centre, I did not. But assistant minister would have known about this, and he would probably use it. We could not communicate in this form, but whether Mr. Kezunovic had used the -- this form or this way of communicating, I don't know. And we, from the communications centres, shouldn't have even known about this, because the dispatch would go to the MUP communications centre, and then they would, if necessary, use this possibility. It is possible that I have seen this document in my contacts with my military communications officers, my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not going to tender that at this time, Your Honour. I would now like to next show the witness 65 ter 2513.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Pejic, this is a -- this appears to be a -- a document, a request for certain information about means and types of communication from -- from the CSB and then a response to that from Vogosca. You're just looking at the first page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall having seen that before today?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: It is already July of 1992, and because of un-uniformed type of equipment that the police stations and communications centres had -- communications centres within the CSBs, it was necessary to make a full review of the equipment at our disposal and to try to either regroup the different devices and to use then uniform equipment. That was the purpose of this proposal. Or, alternatively, to make sure that, in the following period, just as it was before the war, communication devices would be obtained from one type and one brand only, because the engineers and technical staff that were in charge of the maintenance of the system had pointed to us that lack of uniformity of our devices makes it difficult to maintain them or even to obtain the right type of batteries, for instance for radio stations, so this was a review to see what is it that we need for our further work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to the last page. This appears to be the responding information. Do you recognise the signature at the bottom, who that person is?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can recognise it. He worked in the public security station at Vogosca. I do know the name of Rajko Dragicevic. He is responding to the lists of questions I may have asked most probably for some additional information, because this response is not complete. We can see under number 2 that neither the type nor the make of the radio station is listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours I'd like to tender this. I note that the English translation the first name of the signer here is translated as Gojko with a question mark. But I would defer to the witness's identification of the known person. And tender it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1474, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Pejic, do you recall whether Zvornik SJB was a subordinate of the Sarajevo CSB in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have a direct communications link with Zvornik SJB in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Providing there was electrical power available and providing their postal and telephone switchboard was functioning, then we had phone communication, until the high frequency system started functioning against, because before the war, they had been linked up with another node, so although they did have the equipment available, Sarajevo could not have direct communication with Zvornik. Instead, it would have been done at the time through the Sarajevo communications centre which remained in the -- federation part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 46, number -- line 8 and 9, I believe the witness said: We had a phone communication but we didn't have some other kind of communication. So if can you just clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you hear from my learned friend Mr. Zecevic said, and can you help us out with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC
utterances.text: When I was referring to the phone communication, the Zvornik switchboard, if they had power supply, then the phones in Zvornik would be functioning normally. If one phone would be operational, one phone that we had at our communications centre, if that phone could get long distance line or so-called Pale line, we could, at the time, providing that the federal line was not interrupted, we could use phone lines to get in touch with Zvornik.
